sources.title: Search snippet: Agincourt Defence overview and transposition summary (Chessiverse, Wikipedia: Franco-Indian, Catalan, Nimzo-Indian)

overview: Black answers 1.c4 with ...e6, preparing ...d5 with full support and keeping nearly every queen-pawn set-up available. The opening is a transposition magnet: 2.Nc3 d5 gives a QGD-like structure, 2.Nf3 d5 3.g3 a Catalan or Reti, 2.d4 c5 an Anglo-Indian or Queen's Pawn-type game, and 2.e4 a French-like game. Black can also choose Nimzo-Indian or Queen's Indian set-ups after ...Nf6. Play is described as calm, positional and non-forcing; the c8-bishop's development is Black's main early question. Master usage is spread among specialists (Miezis, Uhlmann, Korchnoi, Flear, Sveshnikov, Rozentalis) rather than concentrated, and it is a normal solid choice at every level.

white_ideas.idea: Fianchetto the king's bishop (Nf3, g3, Bg2), a hypermodern framework with control from a distance
Play 2.Nc3 and 3.d4 or 3.e4 to enter a QGD, Nimzo-Indian or French-like game
Transpose into Catalan or Reti structures, or choose English structures with c5 break

black_ideas.idea: Prepare ...d5 with full support and own that square, developing behind the pawn chain
Keep options open: QGD, Catalan, Nimzo-Indian (...Nf6 and ...Bb4) or Queen's Indian (...Nf6 and ...b6)
Meet 2.d4 with ...c5 to challenge the centre immediately
Solve the c8-bishop problem (via ...b6 or ...dxc4 ideas)

typical_structures.structure: Queen's Gambit Declined-type structure (c4/d4 versus e6/d5)
Catalan or Reti fianchetto structures after Nf3 and g3
French-like or Sicilian-adjacent structures after 2.e4 or 2.d4 c5

character.notes: Chessiverse describes 'solid, patient' play and rates sharpness 'Calm' (0.892 at elite level); Wikibooks stresses transpositions into classical frameworks. Typical play is manoeuvring and positional rather than forcing. Risky lines are rare.

gambit.notes: No material is given in the main lines. Queen's Gambit-type pawn offers in transpositions are not true gambits.

soundness.notes: Sound. Chessiverse statistics: White 49.9% wins vs Black 45% across 14.6 million games, with draws rising at higher Elo (10.8% at 2500), suggesting Black's counterplay is easier to find with experience. No source calls it dubious.

structure.notes: Mostly closed or tension-based centre (QGD, Catalan, English structures), with central pawns staying on for a long time. Open centres arise in Catalan lines with ...dxc4 or in the 2.d4 c5 branch; the dominant feel is closed/partly closed.

approach.notes: Described as a 'transposition magnet': Black plays ...e6 and ...d5 against almost any English set-up, a flexible system-like reply. Chessiverse lists strong players as practitioners: Miezis, Uhlmann, Korchnoi (White) and Flear, Sveshnikov, Rozentalis (Black). The reply is respected and normal rather than offbeat; frequency is high (about 14.6 million games in the Chessiverse database).

level.notes: Chessiverse labels it Beginner difficulty. Own understanding: Black has a flexible plan (...d5 supported by ...e6) with relatively little forced theory, but must know several resulting structures (QGD, Catalan, Nimzo) and the c8-bishop issue. Studying side is Black (a defence).

sublines_that_differ.name: 2.d4 c5 (Queen's Pawn/English Anglo-Indian)
sublines_that_differ.how: Immediate challenge to the centre; Sicilian-adjacent / Benoni-like positions.

sublines_that_differ.name: Neo-Catalan
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. c4 e6 2. Nf3 d5 3. g3 Nf6 4. Bg2 Be7 5. O-O
sublines_that_differ.how: Catalan structure with long-term pressure on Black's queenside.

sublines_that_differ.name: 2.e4
sublines_that_differ.how: Transposes to a French-like game; different pawn structures.

description.claim: 1.c4 e6 is known as the Agincourt Defense
description.note: Also called Kurajica Defence per the ECO label.

description.claim: It is a highly flexible and solid system in which Black prepares to challenge for the centre with ...d5
It often transposes into a Queen's Gambit Declined while keeping options for Nimzo-Indian or Queen's Indian set-ups
description.note: Transposition magnet to QGD, Catalan and Reti; Nimzo and Queen's Indian options after ...Nf6.

description.claim: It is positional rather than tactical

common_plans.claim: White often fianchettoes the king's bishop (g3, Bg2), or plays d4 to transpose to Queen's Pawn openings
common_plans.note: g3 set-up and d4 transpositions both named.

common_plans.claim: Black's primary plan is ...d5, often leading to a QGD structure
Black may adopt a hypermodern set-up with ...Nf6 and ...b6 (Queen's Indian) or ...Nf6 and ...Bb4 (Nimzo-Indian)
common_plans.note: Nimzo via 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.d4 Bb4 is cited; the Queen's Indian set-up is cited as a possible transposition.

common_plans.claim: Both sides maneuver for pawn breaks, such as c5 for White or ...c5/...e5 for Black
common_plans.note: ...c5 is cited against 2.d4; the White c5 break and ...e5 are own understanding only.
